title: Merge K Sorted Lists
prompt:
You are given an array of `k` linked lists, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Merge all the lists into one sorted linked list and return its head.

The input is an array of arrays (e.g. `[[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]]` represents three lists `1 -> 4 -> 5`, `1 -> 3 -> 4`, and `2 -> 6`). The starter code includes helpers to convert between arrays and linked-list nodes — build the actual lists, merge them by manipulating `next` pointers (a min-heap over the current heads works well), then convert the result back to a single array to return.

examples.explanation: Merging the three lists together in sorted order.

constraints: Each lists[i] is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Merging two sorted lists at a time is easy — can you repeat that pairwise across all k lists?
A min-heap keyed on node value, storing (value, index, node) for each list's current head, lets you always pop the globally smallest node next.

Because Python's heapq compares tuples element by element and ListNode isn't comparable, include a unique tie-breaker (like the list index or a counter) in the heap tuple to avoid comparing nodes directly.

solution.approach: Convert each input array into a linked list. Push the head of every non-empty list onto a min-heap keyed by (value, unique tiebreaker, node). Repeatedly pop the smallest node, append it to the merged result, and if that node has a next, push it onto the heap. This yields the fully merged, sorted list in O(N log k) time where N is the total number of nodes and k is the number of lists.
solution.timeComplexity: O(N log k), where N is total nodes and k is the number of lists
solution.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the heap (excluding the returned list)
